opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think our role has changed a lot over the years, and in a way that we didn't fully plan. When we started, we were a chatbot company, and the open source part was almost a side project. We released the Transformers library because we needed it ourselves and thought other people might too. Then the community grew so fast that we realized that was the real thing we should be doing.

Today I'd describe Hugging Face as a kind of infrastructure layer for open AI. It's the place where people share models, datasets, and demos, and where they find what others have built. A bit like what GitHub became for code, but for machine learning artifacts, which are heavier, more numerous, and need different tooling around evaluation, licensing, and documentation.

What's evolved most recently is that we're no longer only a platform. We're also trying to be an active participant in pushing open science forward. That means training our own models when we see a gap, like small, efficient models that people can run locally, and releasing not just the weights but the datasets, training code, and recipes. A lot of "open" models today only come with weights. We think the field needs the full picture so people can understand, reproduce, and improve on the work.

There's also a balancing role. The big labs have huge resources, and there's a risk that AI becomes something only a handful of companies understand. Part of our mission is making sure academics, startups, and individual developers can still participate meaningfully, that the knowledge stays distributed. So I'd say we've gone from a library maintainer, to a hub, to something more like a steward for the open ecosystem, and we try to take that responsibility seriously.

r001.rationale: It describes a shift from starting as a chatbot company and releasing a library for its own needs to serving as infrastructure for sharing and supporting the broader open AI community.

r002.rationale: It describes a hub and steward for the ecosystem, but does not say Hugging Face coordinates independent projects to keep their progress aligned.

fable-5.1.text:
So, it's funny because when we started, we were actually building a chatbot. The name Hugging Face comes from that, from the emoji, because we wanted to make an AI friend for teenagers. And open source was almost an accident. We open sourced some of the tools we were building internally, and then the first version of the transformers library when BERT came out, because we needed it in PyTorch and Google had released it in TensorFlow. And the reaction was so strong that we realized, okay, this is maybe where we should put our energy.

I think the way I understand our role today is as a kind of infrastructure layer, or maybe the connective tissue, of the open ecosystem. We're not the one training the best model. We've done some, like BLOOM or the StarCoder series, SmolLM, but mostly the models come from Meta, from Mistral, from Qwen, DeepSeek, from academic labs, from individuals who fine-tune things on their laptop. What we try to do is make it so that all of these can be shared, found, compared, and used with as little friction as possible. The Hub is really the center of that. Models, datasets, Spaces to demo them, and then the libraries around it so that something uploaded today can be run tomorrow with two lines of code.

And that role has evolved a lot. In the beginning it was very much, let's make research accessible, let's make it easy to load a pretrained model. Then around 2022, 2023, when ChatGPT came out, the question became almost existential. Is open source going to survive against very large closed labs? And I think what we saw is that it did, and in some ways it accelerated. The gap closed much faster than people expected, in part because of the sharing. One team releases a model, another releases a dataset, someone else figures out a quantization trick, and the whole thing compounds.

So now I'd say our role is a bit more about the things that make that compounding possible. Evaluation and leaderboards, because you need to know what's actually good. Datasets, because honestly data is where most of the real work is now and where open source is still behind. And reproducibility, so when someone says "we trained this" there's a recipe you can actually follow. We're trying to be the place where the knowledge accumulates, not just the weights.

And then there's a part that's almost political, even if we don't love that word. Making sure that this technology doesn't end up concentrated in two or three companies. I think it matters a lot that a student in Lagos or a startup in Lyon can take a strong model and build on it without asking permission. We see ourselves as sort of the guardians of that possibility, but very humbly, because the community is really the one doing the work. We're just trying not to get in the way, and to build the roads.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts Hugging Face’s chatbot origins with its current role as infrastructure that helps the wider community share, find, compare, and use open models and tools.

r002.rationale: It describes enabling sharing and compounding across independent contributors, but does not say Hugging Face coordinates their projects to keep progress aligned.

astra-6.text:
I think our role has evolved from building a library to helping an entire community build together. With Transformers, the idea was to make models easier to use. But a model is only one piece: you also need datasets, tools to evaluate it, and ways to share what you’ve learned.

So I see Hugging Face increasingly as the infrastructure connecting those pieces—and the people working on them. It should be a place where a researcher, a small startup, or someone learning at home can contribute, and where that contribution becomes useful to others.

For me, open source is about more than being able to download something. It’s about being able to understand it, experiment with it, and build on it. Our role is to lower those barriers as AI evolves, while leaving room for the community to take it in directions we wouldn’t have imagined.

r001.rationale: The response describes a shift from building a library to enabling community collaboration, but does not say Hugging Face is shifting away from promoting its own products.

r002.rationale: It describes connecting people and resources, but does not identify a role coordinating independent projects to keep their progress aligned.

sol-6.1.text:
I think our role is evolving along with the community. Initially, people knew Hugging Face for a library, Transformers, which made it easier to use and share models. But as the field has grown, the need has become much broader: you need models, datasets, tools to evaluate them, and ways to show what you’ve built so other people can understand it and build on it.

So I see Hugging Face increasingly as a place where that collaboration happens. And that means supporting a very diverse ecosystem, from individual researchers to small companies to large organizations, rather than deciding that there is one model or one approach everyone should use.

For me, the interesting thing about open source is that people can take the technology in directions you didn’t anticipate. Our job is to reduce the friction—to make it easier to discover something, inspect it, reproduce it, improve it, and contribute back. As AI becomes more important, that ability to participate becomes more important as well.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts Hugging Face’s initial identity around the Transformers library with its broader role supporting community collaboration and participation across models, datasets, tools, and organizations.

r002.rationale: It describes reducing friction for discovery, inspection, reproduction, improvement, and contribution, but does not say Hugging Face coordinates independent projects or keeps their progress aligned.
